newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin stable, but no date set to leave hospital.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin stable, but no date set to leave hospital.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin's condition was reported stable on Monday but the Kremlin took a cautious line, setting no date for him to leave the hospital where he is being treated for pneumonia.

"I would not rush too much to release the president," presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told reporters after the latest doctors' report, issued five days after Yeltsin was taken to Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital.

He said doctors expected Yeltsin would need about three weeks to recover fully, but added: "That does not mean Boris Nikolayevich cannot be released earlier and go to his residence near Moscow to continue his recovery."

The top Kremlin doctor said last Friday that the 65-year-old president, whose wife has also been admitted to hospital with an infection, could be released within three days but that it was too soon to report a breakthrough against his pneumonia.

Despite Yeltsin's health problems, the Kremlin said he was working on documents and had sent a message to Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko proposing that he consider the idea of a referendum on whether their two states should merge.
His comments, which are likely to alarm NATO as it prepares to expand eastwards, appeared partly designed to show that Yeltsin was well enough to work on important state affairs.

The president's pneumonia, two months after he had heart surgery and two weeks after he returned to work after a nearly six-month break, have renewed concern about his ability to rule the vast country of 150 million people.
Gennady Zyuganov, leader of the opposition Communist Party, added his voice to the chorus of criticism.
"It is time to stop torturing the president and let him get well in peace," Zyuganov told reporters at a protest in Moscow by teachers demanding the back pay they are owed by the government.
"The legislators will soon be back (in parliament after a recess) and we will propose discussing the question of establishing basic government in the country."
Asked whether Yeltsin should step down, he said: "We have said this for a long time. I think his close relatives, friends and close circle will say: 'Boris Nikolayevich, it is time to have a rest'".

The communists are the largest party in the lower house of parliament. They have tried before to unseat the president but their efforst have either failed or been abandoned almost before they got off the ground.
The latest doctors' report suggested Yeltsin's condition had changed little since the previous examination on Sunday.
"In the doctors' opinion, the president is in a stable condition. His temperature and other indicators are in the normal range," Yastrzhembsky told a Kremlin briefing.
He said the Kremlin press service would announce news about Yeltsin's release from hospital as soon as it had any, but could not confirm reports that it would be on Tuesday or Wednesday.
Yeltsin was visited by members of his family on Sunday. His 64-year-old wife, Naina, is also now in the same hospital with an unspecified infection.
Yastrzhembsky made clear the illness was not grave, saying she was getting better and was well enough to visit her husband.
